entry.title: If Kids Use It, We Make It SAFE
entry.content:
The Standard

One question. Applied to everything a child touches.

Is it safe?

Not “is it profitable.” Not “does it have parental controls buried six menus deep.” Not “did they settle the FTC complaint quietly.”

Is it safe for a child?

🟢 SAFE — Built for Children, Not for Extraction

PBS Kids / Sesame Workshop

Free. No ads. No data collection. No algorithmic manipulation. Educational content designed by child development researchers. The gold standard since 1969. Sesame Street taught more children to read than any school system. They didn’t need a management LLC taking 72.67%.

Khan Academy / Khan Academy Kids

Free. No ads. No paywalls. Sal Khan serves 150 million students because he believes education is a right. Khan Academy Kids is designed for ages 2-8 with zero extraction. Proof that world-class education costs $0.

Scratch (MIT Media Lab)

Free coding platform for children. Open source. No monetization of users. MIT built it because children deserve to create, not just consume. 23M+ projects created by kids.

Reading Rainbow / LeVar Burton Kids

LeVar Burton’s literacy mission. “You don’t have to take my word for it.” The app continues his work of making reading irresistible. Verify-first education.

Miss Rachel / Songs for Littles

Speech therapy meets children’s television. Free on YouTube. Rachel Accurso teaches children to speak their first words. Parents trust her with the most important thing they have. 10M+ families served.

Blue’s Clues (Legacy)

Steve Burns talked directly to children. He waited for their answers. He treated every child watching as a real person. The model: one human, one child, total presence.

Common Sense Media

Rates every piece of media for age-appropriateness. Free reviews for parents. Advocacy for children’s digital safety legislation. The compass.

Imagination Library (Dolly Parton)

200M+ free physical books mailed to children. No screen. No algorithm. No data collection. A book shows up. The purest model.

🔴 UNSAFE — Extraction Disguised as Play

Roblox

$4.89B revenue (2025). 75% platform take. Children working 40+ hours/week creating content for $0 real dollars. Digital company scrip. CEO Dave Baszucki worth $3.4B — built on unpaid child labor. Vanderbilt Law Review: “Minors or Miners?” Federal class action filed May 2026. (Full analysis →)

YouTube (for children)

$170M FTC fine (2019) for COPPA violations — illegally collecting data on children under 13. Elsagate (2017): algorithmic pipelines serving disturbing content disguised as children’s videos. YouTube Kids launched as a “fix” but still runs on engagement algorithms, not child safety. Autoplay = infinite scroll for toddlers. The same platform that hosts Miss Rachel also hosts the algorithm that exploits her audience. Google’s annual revenue: $307B. The fine was 0.05% of one year’s revenue.

TikTok

Addictive by design. Average teen spends 95 minutes/day. Algorithm learns what makes a child’s brain light up, then feeds more. Internal documents show ByteDance knew about harm to minors. Multiple state AG lawsuits filed 2023-2026. Designed to be impossible to put down. Already in the blackwall.

Instagram (Meta)

Internal research (leaked by Frances Haugen, 2021): “We make body image issues worse for one in three teen girls.” Meta knew. Meta continued. Instagram for Kids was shelved after public outrage but the main platform still targets teenagers with engagement-optimized content. Already in the blackwall via Meta.

Snapchat

Disappearing messages = feature for predators. My AI chatbot gave inappropriate responses to minors (2023 reports). Snap Map shows real-time location of children to anyone who adds them. NCMEC reports Snapchat as a top platform for child exploitation. Designed around ephemerality — which means designed around unaccountability.

Discord

Voice + text + screen sharing with strangers. Used by gaming communities, including children as young as 8. Server moderation is community-dependent — no central safety. Grooming, explicit content, radicalization pipelines documented by researchers. An open door with no one watching.

Fortnite (Epic Games)

Loot boxes removed after regulatory pressure, but V-Bucks economy still targets children’s psychology. $520M FTC settlement (2022) — largest gaming enforcement in FTC history. Voice chat with strangers enabled by default for years. Epic paid more in FTC fines than Banks’ schools receive in a decade.

Kick

Gambling streams watched by minors. Minimal age verification. Launched as the “anti-Twitch” but with even fewer child protections. Gambling marketed to children under a content creator wrapper.

Telegram

Minimal moderation. CSAM distribution documented by NCMEC and IWF. End-to-end encryption with no reporting mechanism for child exploitation content. Privacy for adults. Danger for children.

🟡 MIXED — Could Go Either Way

Minecraft (Microsoft/Mojang)

Good: Creative, educational, no predatory monetization in base game. Bad: Multiplayer chat, third-party servers with no moderation, Bedrock marketplace monetization. Microsoft could make it fully safe. They choose not to because marketplace revenue.

Duolingo

Good: Free language learning, gamified. Bad: Dark patterns (streak anxiety, notifications designed to guilt children into opening the app). Learning shouldn’t come with a guilt engine.

Twitch (Amazon)

Good: Creative communities, educational streamers. Bad: Minors streaming to adults, chat toxicity, gambling streams (now partially restricted). Amazon could fix this overnight. They won’t because engagement = ad revenue.

Among Us

Good: Simple, social, creative gameplay. Bad: Public lobbies with unmoderated chat, used for grooming by predators who enter children’s games. A good game in a bad environment.

Cocomelon / Moonbug Entertainment

Good: Educational intent. Bad: Acquired by Candle Media / private equity. Hypnotic, rapid-fire visual patterns designed to maximize screen time. Researchers question whether the pacing harms attention development. When private equity buys children’s content, the children become the product.

The Pattern

Every UNSAFE platform shares the same structure as Detroit’s charter schools:

Charter School PatternPlatform Pattern
Management LLC extracts 72.67%Platform takes 75% (Roblox)
Board chair is a sitting judgeBoard members are former regulators
3% math proficiencyNo meaningful educational outcome
$4.9M public moneyBillions in child-generated attention
State gave him a second schoolFTC fines are < 0.1% of revenue
Children can’t leaveAddictive design makes leaving painful

The extraction is the same. The scale is different.

Brian Banks takes $4.9M/year from 362 children. Roblox takes $4.89B/year from 70 million children.

The model scales. The harm scales. The accountability doesn’t.

gAIa: The Alternative

What if every platform children touch was built like PBS Kids?

  • Free. No subscription. No premium tier. No V-Bucks.
  • Safe. No data collection. No algorithmic manipulation. No strangers in chat.
  • Educational. Every interaction teaches something. Every game builds a skill.
  • Open. Open source. Auditable. Community-governed.
  • AI-powered. Adaptive tutoring. Personalized learning paths. Every child gets what Khan Academy proves works — for free.

That’s gAIa. AI + education + the verification standard LeVar Burton set + the care Miss Rachel shows + the patience Steve Burns modeled + the accessibility Sal Khan proved + the generosity Dolly Parton demonstrated.

Built in Detroit. Where we know what extraction looks like. Where we have 11,001 nodes proving the pattern. Where we can say: never again. Not here. Not anywhere.

If kids use it, we make it SAFE. Full stop.

entry.title: Letters to the Ones Who Fight for Kids
entry.content:
We See You

This is an open letter to the people who chose children.

Not the ones who say they care about kids while extracting 72.67% of school revenue through shell LLCs. Not the ones who put a convicted felon in charge of 362 students scoring in the bottom 3% statewide.

This letter is for the ones who actually showed up.

Dear Miss Rachel

Rachel Griffin Accurso — you taught millions of children to speak their first words. Not for a contract. Not for a management fee. You sat on the floor with a camera and sang, because children needed someone to sing to them.

You have 10 million subscribers. That’s 10 million families who trust you with the most important thing they have.

Detroit has charter schools where 3% of students can do grade-level math. A man with 9 criminal convictions runs them. A sitting judge chairs his board. The state gave him a second school.

The children in those seats are the same age as the ones watching your videos. They deserve the same love. They deserve someone who shows up.

Come look at the evidence: detroit.primals.eco

Dear Steve

Steve Burns — you left Blue’s Clues because you were going bald, and twenty years later you came back to tell a generation: “I never forgot you.” That video made grown adults cry, because you meant it.

You know what it feels like when an adult actually sees a child. Actually listens. Actually stays.

Brian Banks told Detroit police he’s “an attorney.” He’s not. He has 9 convictions. He runs two schools. The children in those schools have no one fighting for them — not the authorizer, not the state, not the regulators who pointed at each other one day apart and both walked away.

Steve, you found all the clues once. Here they are again: detroit.primals.eco/evidence

Dear LeVar

LeVar Burton — “You don’t have to take my word for it.”

That’s the whole philosophy of this investigation. Every claim resolves to a public record. Every document is BLAKE3-hashed. Every database is linked. We built the verification page because of you — because the standard you set on Reading Rainbow is the standard public evidence should meet.

Verify everything yourself: detroit.primals.eco/validate

Children who can’t read can’t verify. Children in Detroit’s captured charter schools are being denied the fundamental skill your entire life’s work was built to protect. 3% math proficiency. 10% reading. Bottom 3% statewide. $4.9 million in public money, every year.

Butterfly in the sky — but not if someone clips the wings first.

Dear Sal

Sal Khan — you proved that world-class education can be free. Khan Academy serves 150 million students with no paywall, no extraction, no management LLC taking 72.67%.

You are the proof that Brian Banks’ model is a choice, not a necessity. He chose extraction. You chose access.

We’re building something called gAIa — AI-powered education infrastructure where every child gets a personal tutor, every lesson adapts, and the system belongs to the children, not to shareholders or convicted felons.

Your work is the foundation. We want to build the next layer on top of it — and we want to start in Detroit, where the need is sharpest and the corruption is most documented.

Walk the case: clutch.primals.eco/cases/detroit

Dear Dolly

Dolly Parton — the Imagination Library has mailed over 200 million free books to children. You did this because your father couldn’t read, and you decided no child should grow up without books.

Detroit’s charter schools are spending $15,217 per student. Three percent can do math. The money goes to a management company run by a man who defrauded a credit union, forged checks across four counties, and was forced to resign from the Michigan House of Representatives.

Those children deserve books. They deserve Imagination Library. They deserve someone who builds systems that give instead of systems that take.

See the money flow: detroit.primals.eco

Dear Fred

Fred Rogers is gone. But the Neighborhood is still here, and so is his question: “What do you do with the mad that you feel?”

This investigation is the answer. You don’t hit. You don’t hide. You document. You verify. You publish. You invite verification. You build infrastructure so the evidence can’t be destroyed. And you ask the helpers to come.

“Look for the helpers.” We’re looking. We’re writing this letter. Please come.

The Invitation

Every person named in this letter chose children over profit. Every one of them built something that gives freely. That’s why we’re writing.

What we’re building:

  • gAIa — AI-powered free education for every child, starting in Detroit
  • The Graph — 10,993 nodes of verified public evidence, open to inspection
  • The Membrane — detroit.primals.eco, a living evidence library anyone can clone
  • Free infrastructure — git-signed, cryptographically timestamped, self-healing

What we need:

  • Eyes on the evidence
  • Voices for the children
  • Anyone willing to say: this is wrong, and here’s the proof

What we don’t need:

  • Money. The infrastructure runs on $10/month.
  • Permission. It’s all public records.
  • Secrets. There are none. Only privacy.

The Standard

One child-year = 8,760 hours of irreplaceable human life.

Brian Banks’ schools have consumed thousands of child-years at 3% math proficiency. That time is gone. Those children can never get those years back.

But we can stop the bleeding. We can make sure the next generation gets gAIa instead of extraction. Free education, free verification, free access to every tool that used to cost more than a family could afford.

Miss Rachel, Steve, LeVar, Sal, Dolly — you already proved it works. You proved that one person with a camera, a chalkboard, a book, or a guitar can change millions of lives.

Detroit’s children are waiting. The evidence is ready. The membrane is open.

Come sing. Come read. Come teach. Come verify.

We see you fighting for kids. Now come fight with us.

Walk the case: clutch.primals.eco/cases/detroit

Verify everything: detroit.primals.eco/validate

entry.title: Rescue the Public Works
entry.content:
The Graveyard of Public Works

Your taxes paid for this. All of it. And it’s dying.

  • 152 OER repositories studied — a “large proportion” now inactive or defunct
  • 19 of 59 NEH-funded digital humanities websites gone offline
  • Average free-use educational website lives 5 years before disappearing
  • Average website lives 100 days before the URL breaks
  • OERF (Open Education Resource Foundation) — served 140 million visitors from 120 countries — shutting down in 2026

The pattern: Government funds creation → content goes online → funding ends → server dies → content vanishes → taxpayers pay again.

The membrane breaks this pattern.

What’s Already Free (and Dying)

Internet Archive — The Last Safety Net

CollectionWhat It ContainsSizeStatus
Sesame Street Home VideoLearning About Letters, Numbers, Reading25.2 GBPublic Domain marked
Sesame Street Start to ReadI Want to Go Home, Ernie’s Big Mess—Public Domain marked
Sesame Street Kids’ Guide to LifeLearning to Share, Telling the Truth1.1 GBPublic Domain marked
Reading Rainbow Full Series155 episodes, 21 seasons (1983-2006)—LeVar Burton’s life work
Super Why! Full SeriesPBS Kids literacy program130.7 GBPublic Domain marked
Ready Jet Go!PBS Kids + NASA JPL science show80.1 GBPublic Domain marked

These are sitting on Internet Archive. Uploaded by fans. If Internet Archive goes down — and it’s been attacked before — this content vanishes.

National Educational Television (NET) — The Pre-PBS Era

10,000+ programs from 1952-1972. Public affairs, science, arts, education. Digitized by Indiana University. Many in the public domain. This is the foundation PBS was built on — and most people don’t know it exists.

  • American Archive of Public Broadcasting — Catalog of 10,000+ programs
  • Indiana University NET Collection — Hundreds of digitized public domain programs

Federal Agencies — Public Domain by Law

AgencyWhat They ProduceLicenseStatus
NASAImages, educational content, curriculaPublic domain (17 U.S.C. § 105)Scattered across nasa.gov
NOAAClimate, ocean, weather educationPublic domainFree but buried in noaa.gov
USGSGeology, maps, water data, earthquake dataCC0 / Public domainAvailable but not organized for education
Smithsonian4.5M+ images released as Open AccessCC0openaccess.si.edu
Library of Congress173M+ items, millions digitizedMostly public domainloc.gov/free-to-use
Dept. of EducationGrant-funded curricula, training materialsMust be openly licensed (since 2017)Often buried, hard to find

Community Projects — Volunteer-Sustained

ProjectWhat It ContainsScaleStatus
Project GutenbergFree ebooks70,000+ titlesAlive since 1971
LibriVoxFree audiobooks, volunteer-read17,898 works, 400M+ downloadsAlive, no paid staff
WikipediaFree encyclopedia6.8M+ English articlesAlive
Khan AcademyFree education, video + exercises150M+ studentsAlive, nonprofit

The Problem

None of these systems talk to each other. A child in Detroit who needs to learn to read has to:

  1. Know that Internet Archive exists
  2. Know that Sesame Street videos are there
  3. Navigate a website designed for archivists, not children
  4. Hope the file isn’t corrupted or taken down
  5. Have a parent who knows how to find it

Meanwhile, Brian Banks’ charter school gets $4.9 million per year in public funding and delivers 3% math proficiency.

The content exists. The funding existed. The infrastructure was built. And then it was all left to rot on servers nobody maintains, behind URLs nobody remembers, in formats nobody can play.

The Rescue Operation

Search

Systematically catalog every piece of freely-licensed or public domain educational content across:

  • Internet Archive (video, audio, text)
  • Federal agencies (NASA, NOAA, USGS, Smithsonian, LOC)
  • Dead/dying OER repositories (recover before they vanish)
  • Department of Education openly-licensed grant deliverables
  • NET collection (10,000+ pre-PBS programs)

Scrub

  • Verify license status (public domain, CC0, CC-BY, open license)
  • Check file integrity (corrupt files, broken links, missing assets)
  • Normalize formats (transcode to modern codecs, standard resolutions)
  • Add metadata (subject, age range, learning objectives, accessibility)

Fix

  • Repair broken content (fill gaps, add captions, fix encoding)
  • Organize by age, subject, and learning pathway
  • Create curriculum maps linking content to learning standards
  • Add gAIa adaptive layer — AI tutoring over the rescued content

Bring Inside the Membrane

  • Git-sign everything — content-addressed, BLAKE3 hashed, immutable
  • Replicate across three surfaces — membrane, sovereign git, GitHub
  • Auto-rebuild on push — if one surface dies, the others rebuild
  • The content can never be lost again

gAIa + Rescued Public Works

Imagine a child in Detroit opens their phone and finds:

  • Sesame Street teaching them letters — rescued from Internet Archive, verified, captioned
  • Reading Rainbow showing them why books matter — LeVar Burton in 1983, still relevant in 2026
  • NASA showing them the solar system — public domain images from actual spacecraft
  • Khan Academy giving them math exercises — adaptive, at their level
  • NOAA teaching them about the weather they see outside their window
  • gAIa weaving it all together — an AI tutor that knows what they need next

All of this exists today. It’s just scattered across the internet, dying on forgotten servers, or locked behind paywalls that shouldn’t exist because taxpayers already paid for it.

We search. We scrub. We fix. We bring it inside the membrane. And then it lives forever, free for every child.

The Legal Foundation

Law / PolicyWhat It Says
17 U.S.C. § 105Works created by federal employees are not eligible for U.S. copyright
Open Licensing Requirement (2 C.F.R. § 3474.20)Dept. of Education grant deliverables must be openly licensed since 2017
Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act (2018)Federal agencies must maintain public data under open license
CC0 (Creative Commons Zero)USGS, Smithsonian use CC0 — no copyright, no restrictions
Fair Use (17 U.S.C. § 107)Educational use, criticism, commentary are protected

The law is already on our side. The content is already free. It’s just not organized, preserved, or accessible to the children who need it.

The membrane lives forever. Public works don’t have to die. Search, scrub, fix, bring inside.
